title: India's Rally Defies Global Rout, but Analysts Warn the Rotation Can Reverse
excerpt: Benchmarks are up about 10.5 per cent in seven sessions while the S&P 500 posted its worst week since April 2025. Strategists call it a rotation out of AI stocks, not a decoupling — and say it holds only while the selling stays in technology.
body:
• Indian equities extended their rally on Monday even as global markets sold off sharply, after benchmark indices gained around 10.5 per cent over seven consecutive sessions through Friday.
  • The global rout has been concentrated in AI, semiconductor and data centre stocks: the S&P 500 fell 2.68 per cent last week, its worst week since the April 2025 tariff crash, and Japan and Taiwan slipped into bear markets.
  • Foreign investors have bought Indian shares worth around Rs 37,000 crore so far in November, according to Moneycontrol's analyst coverage.
  • Analysts warn this is rotation, not true decoupling — and rotations can reverse. The shield holds only while global weakness stays confined to AI and US technology stocks.

Indian equity markets traded in positive territory on Monday, extending last week's rally even as global equities witnessed a sharp sell-off — and the question running through dealing rooms is how long the divergence can last.

The global side of the picture is severe. Concerns over artificial intelligence spending and the outcome of the US elections triggered heavy selling worldwide, particularly in AI, semiconductor and data centre stocks. The S&P 500 fell 2.68 per cent, its worst week since the April 2025 tariff crash; Taiwan's index had its steepest weekly fall in two decades; and both Japan and Taiwan slipped into bear markets, according to Moneycontrol's analyst roundup. Against that, India's benchmarks had gained around 10.5 per cent in seven consecutive sessions through Friday, their longest winning streak this year, and foreign investors have purchased Indian shares worth around Rs 37,000 crore in November so far.

Rotation, not decoupling

"India has not decoupled from global markets so much as benefited from a rotation within them, and rotations can reverse just as fast."

— Tanvi Kanchan, Associate Director, Anand Rathi Share and Stock Brokers

That distinction is the analysts' central point. India's outperformance rests on what it does not have: its benchmarks carry little of the AI hardware exposure that dominates the Taiwanese, Korean and Japanese indices, and are weighted instead toward financial services, consumer, energy and industrial companies. Hariselvan Radhakrishnan, founder and CEO of HST Wealth, told Moneycontrol India's resilience is relative rather than absolute, and that the decoupling can hold as long as global weakness remains a rotation out of AI and US technology. Ponmudi R, founder and CEO of Enrich Money, said Indian markets could remain insulated for some time, but not indefinitely — real earnings, domestic consumption and purchasing power will determine long-term strength.

The bigger flow picture

The rotation argument has heavyweight support. JPMorgan's Rajiv Batra told CNBC that if long-term foreign investors merely moved their underweight India positions to neutral, it could translate into roughly $115 billion of potential net inflows — a measure of the possible reallocation, not a forecast. The same CNBC coverage, citing NSDL data, noted foreign investors had net sold more than $31 billion of Indian equities this year through October before turning buyers over the past four trading days with over $2.3 billion of purchases, and that the Nifty 50 rose nearly 9 per cent over the past month while AI-heavy markets fell. Goldman Sachs' Timothy Moe argued India's underlying economic fundamentals are stronger than the simple "anti-AI trade" label suggests.

What would break the shield

The conditions analysts attach to India's resilience are specific: the global sell-off must stay a sector rotation rather than become a broad risk-off move, crude and US yields must stay benign, and foreign inflows must continue. A rotation reverses when the selling broadens — at that point, India's premium valuations, not its index composition, become the story. For now, the flows say the rotation is still running in India's favour.
